title: Gravitational redshift as a quantum channel: modeling the effects of gravitational redshift in quantum optics
authors: Thomas Mieling, Andreas Wolfgang Schell, David Edward Bruschi
abstract: The gravitational frequency shift of light is well understood in the theory of classical electromagnetism. Nevertheless, its description in quantum theory is not yet fully developed. Recent work pointed out inconsistencies in previously developed models aimed at describing gravitational redshift as an effective multi-mode mixer (MMM) acting on modes of light, however, a complete solution of the issues was not obtained. Here, we identify the root cause of the MMM model's inconsistency and provide two complementary approaches to correct it: a "natural" one from a field-theoretic perspective, and another adapted to the language of quantum mechanics of finite-dimensional systems. We show that the second approach allows for modeling of the redshift in a multi-mode transmission setup as a quantum channel that can be characterized using standard quantum information-theoretic techniques when restricting the input states to Gaussian states of light.
summary: This paper addresses the theoretical gap in describing gravitational redshift quantum mechanically. It proves that previous models are inconsistent and resolves this by formulating the effect as a well-defined quantum channel acting on Gaussian states of light. This allows researchers to use modern quantum information tools to analyze relativistic effects on quantum optical signals.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a consistent quantum mechanical description of gravitational redshift, which has historically been modeled using flawed effective multi-mode mixers.
main_result: The authors successfully model the effect as a genuine quantum channel when restricted to Gaussian states, allowing characterization using standard quantum information techniques like fidelity and channel nonunitarity.
method: The work involves analyzing spectral transformations derived from general relativity and correcting inconsistencies in previous models by employing field-theoretic methods and extending the description to unitary channels on larger Hilbert spaces.
model_or_system: The system is light propagating through a stationary spacetime, where the gravitational redshift induces an operator transformation $U_\chi$ on the spectral distribution functions of the photons. The analysis focuses on characterizing this transformation as a quantum channel.
key_observables: Fidelity ($F_\chi$), Channel Nonunitarity ($\eta(\chi)$), and the overlap quantity $\Delta f(\chi) = (f, U_\chi f)$.
important_parameters: The redshift factor $\chi = \sqrt{\zeta_a/\zeta_b}$ dictates the transformation; squeezing in the initial state is crucial for observing fidelity reduction.
main_assumptions:
Previous models incorrectly assumed that the unitary operator $U_\chi$ could be represented by a finite-dimensional matrix, an assumption proven false for general physical spectra when $\chi 
eq 1$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the violation of unitarity ($\gamma_1, \gamma_2$) in older models and show state evolution (e.g., Alice-to-Bob-to-Alice roundtrip) using fidelity measures.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the classical/wave-packet transformation; it then critiques existing multi-mode mixer models, proving their inconsistency; subsequently, it introduces two consistent corrections: a field-theoretic approach and the quantum channel formalism for Gaussian states.
why_interesting: This work bridges general relativity with fundamental quantum information theory by providing rigorous tools (channel nonunitarity) to quantify relativistic effects on quantum light fields, which is highly relevant for quantum communication in curved spacetime.

Here, 𝛼= ln(𝜔0/𝜎) parametrizes the relative width of the Gaussian frequency spectra, where 𝜔0 is the central frequency and 𝜎is the spectral width. As expected, the unitarity of the matrix deteriorates for increasingly sharp Gaussian profiles.

Figure 4. Alice-to-Bob-to-Alice protocol: A photon is sent from Alice to Bob, who receives it in general as a different wave packet (Panel a). Bob measures only the degrees of freedom previously agreed upon with Alice, prepares the new state, and sends it back to Alice (Panel b). Since part of the information is in general lost to unobservable modes, Alice will not receive the same wave packet as the one that she had sent (Panel c). The picture is for illustrative purposes only: the space-time is static and, in general, the round-trip protocol is best implemented using a ground station and a static rocket.
